newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian govt wins confidence vote on immigrant law.
newsitem.headline: Italian govt wins confidence vote on immigrant law.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government won a confidence vote in parliament on Wednesday on a draft law designed to allow some 250,000 previously illegal immigrants to stay in the country.
Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano had sought the vote in the Senate (upper house) to overcome filibustering from hard right opponents of the bill.

The victory, by 163 votes to 106, swept away some 7,000 blocking amendments, nearly all of them submitted by the hard-right National Alliance party, and meant the draft bill was approved by the Senate.

The bill now moves to the lower house where Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition may have to resort to another confidence test unless National Alliance, which has long argued for the expulsion of all illegal immigrants, changes tactics.
The party, which had submitted 6,018 amendments to the draft law, earlier called the decision to resort to a confidence vote an affront to parliament.

"It is yet another demonstration of the Soviet-style arrogance of the Prodi government, which is preventing the opposition from carrying out its constitutional role," senior National Alliance politician Maurizio Gasparri said.
Thousands of immigrants, many from Africa, Albania and the Philippines, enter Italy without visas or work papers, often on small boats from across the Adriatic or from North Africa.

They were given a chance to regularise their status under a partial amnesty last November, when the then government issued a decree allowing illegal immigrants already in the country to remain as long as they registered with police.

The stop-gap measure, never converted into law, has been re-issued five times but cannot be rolled over again. The vacuum has raised doubts about whether foreigners who took advantage of the measures are now safe from possible expulsion.
The draft law will ensure that foreigners who have already registered can stay in Italy once it is approved.
It also allows for the expulsion without appeal of illegal immigrants who are deemed a public security risk and stiff fines for Italians who employ unregistered foreigners.
The anti-racist group SOS Razzismo welcomed the government's decision to put the issue to a confidence test.

"The 255,000 requests to be regularised that were presented under the...amnesty require a just response," the group said in a statement. "The credibility of our institutions is at stake and our heritage as a people of emigrants," it said.
The Constitutional Court last month banned the practice by which successive governments have re-issued decrees, which lapse after 60 days unless they are passed into law by parliament.
The ruling has forced Prodi's government to put several decrees to confidence votes to rush them into law or to replace them by draft laws.
Napolitano told the Senate that the law applied only to foreigners who had legalised their position under the decrees.
He said it would not prejudice consideration by parliament of longer-term regulations on immigration, which he said the government would present early next year.
